separable: inseparable — the place always follows the whole phrase: *hails from Ohio*, never ✗ *hails Ohio from*.
transitivity: transitive — always with a place after *from*
gloss: To come originally from a particular place.
examples: Both finalists *hail from* small towns in Iowa.
Her grandparents *hailed from* a village outside Naples.
The band, *hailing from* Detroit, sold out the show in an hour.
contrast: Used of people and of things with an origin story (*a recipe hailing from Sicily*), not of ordinary travel: you *come from* the store, you do not ✗ *hail from* it.

separable: inseparable — the system follows the whole phrase: *hacked into the server*, never ✗ *hacked the server into*.
gloss: To break into a computer system without permission.
examples: Someone *hacked into* the district's grading system.
Thieves are *hacking into* accounts with passwords stolen years ago.
He only *hacks into* systems he is paid to test.
contrast: The object is the system, not the person: *hack into her account*, never ✗ *hack into her*.

separable: separable — *hammer out a deal* and *hammer the deal out* are both fine; with a pronoun it must split: *hammer it out*, never ✗ *hammer out it*.
gloss: To reach an agreement or a plan after long, difficult discussion.
examples: The two sides *hammered out* a contract at four in the morning.
We still need to *hammer out* who pays for shipping.
They have been *hammering out* the details all week.

separable: separable — *hammer home the point* or *hammer the point home*; with a pronoun it must split: *hammer it home*.
gloss: To repeat a point forcefully until everyone understands it.
examples: The coach *hammered home* the same lesson at every practice.
She *hammers* the point *home* with one number: forty percent.
The campaign is *hammering home* a single slogan.

separable: separable — *hand down a name*, *hand the recipe down*; with a pronoun it must split: *hand it down*. Very often passive: *handed down from her grandmother*.
gloss: To pass something to a younger generation.
examples: The watch was *handed down* from his grandfather.
She *hands down* every winter coat to her younger sister.
Families here have been *handing down* the same recipes for a century.

separable: separable in form — *hand the sentence down* — but in this legal sense it is usually left whole: *hand down a ruling*; with a pronoun it splits: *hand it down*.
gloss: To announce an official decision or sentence, as a court does.
examples: The Supreme Court *handed down* its decision on Thursday.
No one knows when the judge will *hand down* a sentence.
The panel has *handed down* tougher penalties since the rule changed.

separable: separable — *hand in your homework* and *hand your homework in* are both fine; with a pronoun it must split: *hand it in*, never ✗ *hand in it*.
gloss: To give a piece of work or a formal document to someone in authority.
examples: *Hand in* your tests when the bell rings.
He *handed in* his resignation on Monday.
She has already *handed* her application *in*.
contrast: *Hand in* goes up to a teacher or a boss; *hand out* goes around to a group. Same verb, opposite direction.

separable: separable — *hand off the project*, *hand the project off*; with a pronoun it must split: *hand it off*.
gloss: To pass a task, a duty, or the ball to someone else.
examples: I'm *handing off* the account to Marcus on Friday.
The quarterback *handed* the ball *off* and got flattened.
Once the code is tested, it gets *handed off* to support.

separable: separable — *hand out the papers*, *hand the papers out*; with a pronoun it must split: *hand them out*.
gloss: To give something to each person in a group.
examples: Volunteers *handed out* bottled water at every mile.
Could you *hand out* these worksheets?
They were *handing* free samples *out* by the entrance.

separable: separable — *hand over the keys*, *hand the keys over*; with a pronoun it must split: *hand them over*.
gloss: To give something or someone to another person, usually because you have no choice.
examples: The robber told him to *hand over* his wallet.
She *handed over* the keys and called a cab.
Power was peacefully *handed over* in January.

separable: fixed — *it* never changes and never moves, and the person follows *to*: *you have to hand it to her*, never ✗ *hand her it*.
gloss: To admit that someone deserves credit for something.
examples: You have to *hand it to* her — she never misses a deadline.
I've got to *hand it to* the kid; that was a great catch.
Even his critics *handed it to* him after the speech.
contrast: Almost always after *have to* or *got to*: *you have to hand it to them*. A bare *I hand it to them* sounds wrong.

ru: твердить одно и то же, зудеть; долдонить
separable: inseparable — the topic follows the whole phrase: *harp on the same thing*, never ✗ *harp the same thing on*.
transitivity: transitive — always with *on* before the topic
gloss: To keep talking about the same complaint until it annoys people.
examples: He *harps on* my spending every time we go out.
She *harped on* the mistake for weeks.
Quit *harping on* the past.
contrast: Always disapproving — you *harp on* a grievance, never on good news.

ru: обсуждать, обсудить во всех деталях; утрясать, утрясти
separable: separable — *hash out the details*, *hash the details out*; with a pronoun it must split: *hash it out*.
gloss: To talk something through at length until the details are settled.
examples: Let's *hash out* the schedule over lunch.
They *hashed out* their differences in the parking lot.
We're still *hashing out* who drives.
contrast: *Hash* takes *-es*: *hashes out*. Close to *hammer out*, but *hash out* is the talking; *hammer out* is the deal that comes of it.

separable: n/a — intransitive, so nothing can come between the parts; a destination takes *to*: *head back to the hotel*.
gloss: To start traveling back toward the place you came from.
examples: We should *head back* before it gets dark.
They *headed back* to the campsite at sunset.
I'm *heading back* on the six o'clock train.

separable: separable — *head off a strike*, *head the problem off*; with a pronoun it must split: *head it off*.
gloss: To stop something bad from happening by acting before it does.
examples: The company raised wages to *head off* a strike.
A quick apology *headed off* a much bigger fight.
They're *heading off* complaints by refunding everyone.

ru: перехватывать, перехватить; преграждать путь, преградить путь
separable: separable — *head off the runner*, *head the runner off*; with a pronoun it must split: *head him off*.
gloss: To get in front of someone in order to stop them from going where they were going.
examples: Two deputies *headed off* the truck at the county line.
If we cut across the field, we can *head* them *off*.
She was *headed off* by reporters before she reached her car.

separable: n/a — intransitive, so nothing splits it; a destination takes *for* or *to*: *head out for the lake*.
gloss: To leave a place and set off somewhere.
examples: We're *heading out* at six to beat the traffic.
He *headed out* without saying goodbye.
*Head out* early if you want a parking spot.
contrast: *Head out* is leaving; *head off* is stopping something. Do not swap them: ✗ *I'm heading off a strike at six*.

separable: separable in form — *head the committee up* is possible — but it is nearly always left whole: *head up the committee*. With a pronoun it does split: *she heads it up*.
gloss: To be in charge of a group, a team, or a project.
examples: She *heads up* the marketing team.
He *headed up* the investigation for two years.
A former teacher is *heading up* the new program.

ru: двигаться к, идти к; неминуемо приближаться (к чему-то плохому)
separable: inseparable — the outcome follows *for*: *heading for trouble*, never ✗ *heading trouble for*. Most often in the form *be headed for*.
transitivity: transitive — always with *for* before the outcome
gloss: To be on course for a particular result, usually a bad one.
examples: The talks are *heading for* collapse.
We were *headed for* a shutdown until the last-minute deal.
Analysts say the economy could *head for* a slowdown next year.
contrast: *Headed for* in this sense is not a passive: *we were headed for trouble* means we were going toward it, not that someone directed us.

separable: n/a — intransitive here; the wound is the subject, not an object: *the burn is healing up*.
gloss: To get completely better, of a wound or an injury.
examples: The cut *healed up* in a week.
Give it time and the blister will *heal up* on its own.
His shoulder is finally *healing up*.

sense: make food or a place warm
separable: separable — *heat up the soup*, *heat the soup up*; with a pronoun it must split: *heat it up*, never ✗ *heat up it*.
transitivity: both — transitive (heat up the leftovers), intransitive (the oven heats up fast)
gloss: To make something warm again, or to become warm.
examples: I'll *heat up* the leftovers.
She *heated* the sauce *up* while the pasta boiled.
The oven is still *heating up*.

separable: n/a in this sense — it takes no object: *the race heated up*.
gloss: To become more intense, more exciting, or more hostile.
examples: The race *heated up* after the second debate.
Things are *heating up* between the two companies.
Competition *heats up* every year around the holidays.

separable: separable — *help out a friend* or *help your sister out*; with a pronoun it must split: *help me out*, never ✗ *help out me*.
transitivity: both — transitive (help a neighbor out), intransitive (she helps out on weekends)
gloss: To give someone help, especially with work, money, or a favor.
examples: Could you *help* me *out* with the dishes?
His parents *helped* him *out* with the down payment.
She has been *helping out* at the food bank since March.
contrast: *Help out* is a hand given in passing; plain *help* is broader. The thing you help with takes *with*: *help me out with the rent*.

ru: угощаться, угоститься; брать самому, взять самому
separable: fixed — the reflexive pronoun matches the subject (*help myself / yourself / themselves to*), and the thing always follows *to*.
transitivity: transitive — with a reflexive pronoun and *to*
gloss: To take as much of something as you want without waiting to be served.
examples: *Help yourself to* whatever's in the fridge.
He *helped himself to* three slices before anyone sat down.
Guests were *helping themselves to* the buffet.
contrast: Said of someone else's property it is sarcastic: *he helped himself to the petty cash* means he stole it.

separable: separable — *hem in the valley*, *hem the horses in*; with a pronoun it must split: *hem them in*. Usually passive: *hemmed in by rules*.
gloss: To surround someone or something so closely that movement or choice is limited.
examples: Mountains *hem in* the valley on three sides.
We were *hemmed in* by traffic for an hour.
New rules are *hemming in* small landlords.
contrast: The *m* doubles before an ending: *hemmed in*, *hemming in* — one *m* would read as *heeming*.

separable: separable — *hitch up the trailer*, *hitch the trailer up*; with a pronoun it must split: *hitch it up*.
gloss: To attach a trailer or an animal to whatever will pull it.
examples: He *hitched up* the camper before sunrise.
We *hitch* the boat *up* every Friday in the summer.
They were *hitching up* the horses when the rain started.
contrast: *Hitch* takes *-es*: *hitches up*. Of clothes it means to pull them higher: *he hitched up his pants*.

separable: n/a — intransitive, so nothing splits it; the place takes *in*: *hole up in a motel*.
gloss: To shut yourself away somewhere for a while, hiding or avoiding people.
examples: The suspect *holed up* in a cabin for three days.
I'm going to *hole up* at home and finish the draft.
They have been *holed up* in the office since Monday.
contrast: *Holed up* looks passive but is not: *he was holed up* describes where he was, not something done to him.

separable: separable — *hollow out the middle class*, *hollow the town out*; with a pronoun it must split: *hollow it out*. Often passive: *hollowed out by cuts*.
gloss: To weaken something from the inside until little of substance is left.
examples: Decades of layoffs *hollowed out* the town.
Automation is *hollowing out* middle-income jobs.
The agency has been *hollowed out* by budget cuts.

ru: нацеливаться на, нацелиться на; сосредоточиваться на, сосредоточиться на
separable: inseparable — the target follows the whole phrase: *home in on the problem*, never ✗ *home the problem in on*.
transitivity: transitive — always with *in on* before the target
gloss: To move or focus closely toward one target or one detail.
examples: Investigators *homed in on* a single email.
The camera *homes in on* one face in the crowd.
She's *homing in on* the cause of the bug.
contrast: *Home in on*, not ✗ *hone in on* — *hone* means to sharpen a blade. The image is a homing pigeon.

separable: separable — *hook up the speakers*, *hook the speakers up*; with a pronoun it must split: *hook it up*, never ✗ *hook up it*.
gloss: To connect a machine to power, to a network, or to another machine.
examples: Can you *hook up* the speakers?
He *hooked* the trailer lights *up* in five minutes.
They're *hooking up* the new washer tomorrow.

separable: n/a — intransitive; the other person follows *with*: *hook up with Dan after work*.
gloss: To meet someone informally, usually by arrangement.
examples: Let's *hook up* after the game.
We *hooked up* with the others at the trailhead.
I'm *hooking up* with my cousins in Denver.
contrast: Risky in American English: with a person of the age and sex you might date, *hook up with* is usually heard as the sexual sense. Say *meet up with* when you mean only meeting.

ru: мутить, замутить (разг.); вступать в случайную связь
separable: n/a — intransitive; the other person follows *with*: *hooked up with someone from work*.
gloss: To have a casual sexual encounter with someone, in informal American speech.
examples: They *hooked up* after the party and never spoke again.
Everyone assumes those two are *hooking up*.
She *hooked up with* someone from her chemistry class.
contrast: Slang, and the default reading among younger Americans — which is why *I hooked up with my boss* is a sentence to avoid unless you mean it.

ru: подгонять, подогнать (разг.: доставать, достать); выручать, выручить
separable: separable — the person is the object and normally sits inside: *hook me up*, *hook my brother up with a ticket*; the thing follows *with*.
gloss: To get someone something they want, or to put them in touch with it.
examples: My cousin *hooked* me *up* with tickets.
The manager *hooks up* regulars with free refills.
He's *hooking* us *up* with a ride to the airport.
contrast: Informal, and the person always comes first: *hook me up with a job*, never ✗ *hook a job up with me*.

separable: n/a — intransitive; it takes no object at all.
gloss: To play roughly or fool around instead of being serious.
examples: Quit *horsing around* — dinner's ready.
The boys *horsed around* in the pool all afternoon.
He *horses around* in class and then wonders why his grades slip.

ru: сбиваться в кучу, сбиться в кучу; собираться в кружок, собраться
separable: n/a — intransitive; people *huddle up*, and no object can come between the parts.
gloss: To gather closely together, for warmth or for a quick private talk.
examples: The team *huddled up* before the last play.
We *huddle up* for five minutes every morning.
They were *huddling up* under one blanket.

separable: n/a — intransitive; no object can come between the parts.
gloss: To settle into one place and stay there through something difficult.
examples: Residents *hunkered down* as the hurricane came ashore.
We're *hunkering down* for a long negotiation.
She *hunkers down* in the library every finals week.
contrast: *Hunker* survives almost nowhere else in American English — it is heard in *hunker down* and little besides.

separable: separable — *hunt down the suspect*, *hunt the suspect down*; with a pronoun it must split: *hunt them down*.
gloss: To search for someone or something persistently until you find them.
examples: It took a week to *hunt down* the receipt.
Police *hunted down* the driver in two days.
She has been *hunting down* a replacement part for months.
contrast: *Hunt down* ends in success; *hunt for* is only the searching: *I hunted for my keys all morning*.

separable: separable when there is an object — *hurry the kids up*, *hurry up the order*; with a pronoun it must split: *hurry him up*. Most often there is no object at all: *hurry up, we're late*.
transitivity: both — intransitive (hurry up!), transitive (hurry the kids up)
gloss: To move or act faster, or to make someone else do so.
examples: *Hurry up* — the movie starts in ten minutes.
She *hurried* the kids *up* and out the door.
He's *hurrying up* to catch the last bus.
contrast: The *-y* changes before an ending: *hurries up*, *hurried up*, but *hurrying up* keeps it.

separable: separable — *hush up the scandal*, *hush the story up*; with a pronoun it must split: *hush it up*.
gloss: To keep something embarrassing secret by stopping people from talking about it.
examples: The district tried to *hush up* the report.
They *hushed* the whole thing *up* for a decade.
Nothing gets *hushed up* in a town this size.
contrast: *Hush* takes *-es*: *hushes up*. As an order to a person it is a different, much softer thing: *hush up and listen* just means be quiet.

separable: separable — *hype up the movie*, *hype the movie up*; with a pronoun it must split: *hype it up*.
gloss: To promote something loudly, making it sound better than it is.
examples: The studio *hyped up* the sequel for a year.
Don't *hype* it *up* too much or people will be disappointed.
Everyone's *hyping up* the new phone.
contrast: Drop the silent *e* before an ending: *hyped up*, *hyping up*.

separable: separable — *hype up the crowd*, *hype the crowd up*; with a pronoun it must split: *hype them up*. Common as an adjective: *the kids are all hyped up*.
gloss: To make someone excited and full of nervous energy.
examples: The DJ *hyped up* the crowd before the main act.
He *hypes* himself *up* with the same playlist before every game.
The kids were all *hyped up* on sugar by four o'clock.
